newsitem.title: MEXICO: Fed policy has lowered natural jobless rate - Jordan.
newsitem.headline: Fed policy has lowered natural jobless rate - Jordan.

text.p: The Federal Reserve's successful anti-inflation monetary policy has allowed the natural rate of U.S. unemployment to drop to levels that would have been deemed inflationary in the past, said Jerry Jordan, President of the Cleveland Fed.

"Sometimes, the commentaries we see have the causality reversed. They tend to say that because we had strong employment growth, we run the risk of inflation, while it is the other way around," Jordan told Reuters.

"Because we had low inflation, because our credibility is building, that is why you have such a low unemployment rate," Jordan said, answering a question on the relevance of the unemployment rate as a factor in U.S. monetary policy.

Jordan spoke to Reuters in an interview conducted after an economic conference held here from November 27 to December 1. The conference was hosted by a business group, Instituto Mexicano de Ejecutivos de Finanzas.
One popular economic theory pegs the so-called natural rate of unemployment--the supposed long-term minimum without higher inflation--at 5.75 percent.
But U.S. unemployment has averaged about 5.5 percent over the past two years while inflation has held nearly flat.
Jordan called the low jobless rate "the dividend we get for the hard work of building up our credibility with the people."
The Cleveland Fed president disparaged the notion that a low unemployment rate raises inflation and that the Fed's anti-inflation stance thus restrains job creation.
He added that low inflation expectations foster optimal conditions for businesses to expand and thus create jobs.
Jordan said this view is widely held at the policy-setting Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC).

"Everyone (at the FOMC) has spoken on the issue that the ultimate objective of monetary policy is maximum sustainable prosperity, which means the highest rates of growth, of employment, productivity, capital formation and standards of living," Jordan said.
"By being pro-job creation in the long run, of course, they (FOMC members) are not anti-jobs," Jordan stressed, while noting policy makers may express this view in different ways.
"(New York Fed President) Bill McDonough, (San Francisco Fed President) Bob Parry or Chairman (Alan) Greenspan--they would say 'I'm for the maximum rate of growth,'" Jordan noted.
"The Federal Reserve's view... is that a low or no inflation environment is the best condition for maximum sustainable growth," Jordan added.

Jordan, whose address to the conference centered on job creation, said an unsustainably low unemployment rate may result from government programs aimed at artificially creating jobs in specific sectors, such as defense.

"We have seen times in our history when you have certain kind of government programs designed to stimulate certain types of jobs above a long-term sustainable rate," the Cleveland Fed president said. "When the government program ends, those people have periods of unemployment. The best example is defense."
But Jordan also asserted that governments can play an important role in long-term job creation through education and training programs that "give people marketable skills." -- 212-859-1666
